540.bp: Online shopping and streaming sites show you things they think you'll like, but they struggle when someone is brand new to a platform or when they need to recommend products across completely different datasets. This paper asks: can we borrow the recipe that made large language models successful—feeding them enormous amounts of mixed-up data from many sources—and use it to make recommendations smarter and faster?
540.wh: The obvious move is to train a recommendation system on one dataset at a time, but this misses a huge opportunity: each dataset captures different signals (images, prices, descriptions, user behavior). Moreover, when someone is new to a platform, there's almost no history to go on. Traditional systems learn specialized patterns per dataset, but those patterns stay locked inside; when you switch to a new dataset or new user, the system has to start from scratch.
540.ap: RecCLIP reformulates the recommendation problem as a visual-language alignment task. Instead of treating a user's interest as abstract numbers, it converts what a person likes into visual pictures that a vision-language model can understand, then uses simple prompt-based ranking to say 'show me the top matches.' The key is combining many recommendation datasets at once during training so the model sees patterns across all of them simultaneously.
540.ww: When a neural system sees a diverse diet of examples—many datasets, many types of signals—it builds more flexible inner representations that generalize. A new user or a new dataset doesn't break the system because the model has already learned what 'similar' means across hundreds of thousands of examples. Scaling up data this way mirrors how language models work: more data and variety beats more complexity.
540.po: Experiments show the system improves significantly on the two hardest problems in recommendations: cold-start (new users with no history) and cross-domain transfer (predicting what a music fan will like when they switch to a furniture shopping site). The improvement follows a power-law relationship—feeding it twice as much data yields meaningful gains each time, just like language models do.

541.bp: When a geopolitical crisis erupts in the Middle East—a war, a blockade, a coup—predicting what happens next is literally a matter of lives and livelihoods. But current AI prediction systems treat forecasting as a single straight-line path from known facts to a single predicted outcome, which flattens the genuine complexity of international relations.
541.wh: The Middle East involves layers of history, competing interests among many nations, cultural and religious context, and cascades of unexpected events that ripple outward. A single AI model that outputs one timeline has no way to consider that multiple futures are genuinely possible or that different expert analysts—someone steeped in Iranian politics, someone in Gulf economics, someone tracking military capabilities—would naturally disagree and refine their thinking together.
541.ap: ThinkTank-ME runs multiple specialized large language models (one tuned on Iranian geopolitics, another on Gulf economics, etc.) in parallel, each making its own forecast. Then these 'experts' critique and challenge each other's reasoning, revising their predictions as they debate. The system also came with a new benchmark dataset specifically for Middle East event forecasting to measure whether this approach actually works.
541.ww: Disagreement and debate force each model to articulate *why* it believes what it believes. When one expert says 'the price of oil will drop,' another can ask 'because what happens to Saudi production?' This back-and-forth sharpens reasoning and reveals blind spots no single model would catch. Real expert panels work this way; collaborative models mimic that rigor.
541.po: The multi-expert debate approach outperforms single-model systems at predicting real Middle East events. By measuring against actual crises that occurred after August 2024, the researchers showed that the collaborative reasoning genuinely captures geopolitical nuance that monolithic predictions miss.

542.bp: Imagine a doctor needs answers from a 200-page medical guideline, or a lawyer must extract key precedents from case law. Systems that pull information from documents struggle because breaking a document into chunks destroys the context that makes information actually make sense. A diagnostic finding makes sense only in the context of the full case history; a legal clause depends on surrounding agreements.
542.wh: If you simply split documents into equal-sized pieces or cut at sentence boundaries, you lose the semantic backbone that held information together. A question like 'what is the standard treatment?' might end up split across three chunks, or entirely missing because the answer spans a concept nobody indexed. Domain documents are especially dense—every sentence interconnects with others, so naive chunking explodes the complexity.
542.ap: QChunker treats text chunking as a two-step process: first, identify the logical boundaries where meaning naturally breaks (text segmentation). Second, fill in gaps and add context to make each chunk self-contained (knowledge completion). A pipeline of four specialized components does this: one generates an outline of questions implicit in the document, another segments the text based on that structure, a third checks each chunk for logical integrity, and a fourth patches in missing connective information. The system learned this process on 45,000 hand-curated examples.
542.ww: Documents have a hidden logical structure that mirrors how we ask questions about them. If you build chunking around the questions people actually ask, the pieces naturally align with meaning. Adding back context and completing partial concepts ensures that each chunk stands alone without forcing the downstream reader to puzzle out missing pieces. This turns document fragmentation into document understanding.
542.po: When the system retrieves text to answer questions, it has to work with fewer, higher-quality chunks. This reduces the amount of information the language model must sift through, making answers faster and more accurate. The researchers validated their approach on question-answering tasks, showing that domain-specific chunking outperforms off-the-shelf methods.

543.bp: Edge devices—phones, IoT sensors, embedded systems in factories—need to learn and adapt over their lifetime, picking up new tasks without replacing the hardware. But these devices have tiny brains: a model with billions of parameters won't fit. Engineers shrink models by removing unnecessary parts (pruning), but this creates a Catch-22: a pruned model learns new skills slowly.
543.wh: When a neural network encounters a stream of new tasks—'learn to recognize cats, now learn dogs, now learn birds'—it often forgets how to adapt altogether, a problem called plasticity loss. Meanwhile, model pruning removes connections in the network to save space and power. These two problems collide: a tiny pruned model is doubly handicapped at learning anything new because it has few connections left to rewire.
543.ap: PaCP operates in two phases. Before deployment, it prunes the model but does so in a way that preserves the capacity to adapt, using a metric that measures how easily a model can learn new tasks. Later, when the device encounters a new task, the model temporarily adds back some connections to give itself more flexibility for learning. Once the new skill is learned, it prunes away the temporary connections again to return to the tiny form.
543.ww: Plasticity—the ability to learn—lives in the connections between neurons. Rather than destroying important learning-capacity connections upfront, the system cuts the ones that matter less for future adaptation, then recovers flexibility on demand. This is like keeping a toolbox compact but reserving certain tools so you can pop them back in when you need to fix something new.
543.po: Experiments show that PaCP models learn new tasks nearly as well as unpruned models, yet stay small enough to run on embedded hardware. Remarkably, they even beat some non-pruned baselines on continual learning benchmarks, suggesting that strategic pruning and adaptive expansion actually improve learning flexibility.

544.bp: When a company faces a PR crisis—a scandal, a product failure, a viral backlash—public opinion shifts rapidly and unpredictably. What people actually think is a mix of immediate emotional reactions ('that's outrageous!') layered onto deeper beliefs ('I don't trust this company anyway'). Understanding both layers is essential for damage control and authentic recovery.
544.wh: Existing prediction systems treat opinion as a single thread or snapshot, missing how emotions and underlying beliefs constantly push and pull on each other. In a crisis, someone's initial fury might soften if the company responds transparently, or harden if they feel dismissed. Models that ignore this interplay—that separate hot emotion from cool reasoning—can't track why opinion actually shifts.
544.ap: DualMind runs multiple language models to simulate different people discussing the crisis in real time. Each agent has both emotional and cognitive layers: the emotional layer captures immediate reactions ('this is terrible for customers'), while the cognitive layer maintains persistent views ('I always knew this company cut corners'). These two systems interact—emotions can change beliefs, and beliefs color how emotions are expressed—across a simulation that unfolds like actual social media conversation.
544.ww: Real human opinion isn't mechanical. A fact doesn't just update belief coldly; it hits our emotions first. A company's authentic apology might lower our anger, which then allows our underlying doubts to settle. By separating and connecting emotion and cognition, the simulation mimics the psychological depth of actual belief formation.
544.po: When tested against real crisis data from social media (15 actual crises post-August 2024), DualMind predicted public opinion trajectories far more accurately than single-layer systems. The model captured the back-and-forth of real crisis dynamics—spikes of outrage, gradual cooling, shifts in credibility—that simpler systems miss.

545.bp: Short-video platforms like TikTok and Reels engineer their algorithms to keep people watching—and some users watch for hours until exhaustion, often against their own intentions. Understanding exactly how these platforms can pull someone into unhealthy patterns, and how to break those patterns without destroying the platform, is a crucial question for public health.
545.wh: Most research on addiction relies on surveys ('Do you think you use TikTok too much?'), which capture self-awareness but are small-scale and biased toward people willing to admit problems. The platform itself has the real data—millisecond-by-millisecond records of clicks, watches, rewatches, and pauses—but that data stays private and goes unutilized for understanding addiction mechanics.
545.ap: AddictSim borrows from economics the theory of how addiction actually works: consumption increases short-term reward but also builds tolerance, so the person must consume more to get the same hit. The researchers analyzed real platform behavior data—millions of user sessions—and found it matches this economic model. Then they built a simulator that learns each person's unique addiction pattern and predicts how they'll respond to algorithmic changes (showing more diverse content, throttling recommendations, etc.).
545.ww: Economic addiction theory gives a concrete mechanism: the brain's reward system adapts to stimulus. What thrills you on day one bores you by day thirty, so you seek stronger stimulus. Short-video platforms exploit this because new videos are always available. By mapping real behavior onto this well-studied mechanism, the simulator can predict counterfactuals: what if we changed the algorithm?
545.po: Simulations show that inserting diversity-aware algorithms—deliberately mixing in unexpected content rather than endlessly serving what usually hooks each person—can break addictive patterns without killing engagement. The system provides a tool for platform designers to test interventions before deployment, potentially reducing harm without sacrificing business models.

546.bp: When hurricanes, earthquakes, or famines strike, humanitarian organizations need to know exactly where people are suffering to allocate aid. Geographic databases exist, but they often miss regions in the Global South or encode Western geography as default, leaving crisis-hit areas invisible and aid underdirected.
546.wh: Automated systems that extract location names from text have been trained mostly on Western data, so they recognize 'Boston' instantly but struggle with 'Hargeisa' (Somaliland). Also, many place names are ambiguous: 'Paris' could be Paris, France or Paris, Texas. Rule-based systems guess poorly. Larger language models could help, but if they inherit the same geographic biases, they'll just perpetuate invisibility.
546.ap: The paper combines two techniques: few-shot learning from a language model (showing it just a handful of examples of location extraction), and then a reasoning step where the model uses surrounding context to figure out which 'Paris' makes sense. For instance, if the text says 'Paris was damaged by heavy rains in the Midwest,' the system recognizes the Midwest as context and correctly identifies Paris, Texas, not Paris, France.
546.ww: Large language models encode world knowledge about place names and their contexts. By giving them just a few examples and letting them reason about context, they overcome both training bias and ambiguity. The reasoning step is crucial: the model doesn't just guess; it actually thinks about what other place-related information is present in the document.
546.po: Tests on humanitarian documents show that LLM-based extraction dramatically outperforms traditional systems on both accuracy and fairness. Underrepresented regions—areas in Africa, South Asia, Latin America—see much higher detection rates, meaning aid organizations can now identify crisis zones they previously missed. This directly improves where humanitarian resources flow.

547.bp: WebAssembly is a technology that lets developers write code once and run it anywhere—in a browser, on a server, on any device that speaks WebAssembly. But when the same code runs as native (traditional machine code) versus WebAssembly, it sometimes produces different results, silently breaking real applications.
547.wh: Converting code from native format to WebAssembly touches dozens of low-level details: how numbers are represented, how memory is organized, how system calls work. Each difference is tiny, but they accumulate. A floating-point calculation might round differently; memory alignment might shift. These discrepancies are hard to spot because the program still runs; it just gives wrong answers on some inputs.
547.ap: WasmDiff is an automated testing framework that runs the same code as both native and WebAssembly with thousands of test inputs, comparing the outputs line by line. Whenever the native version and WebAssembly version produce different results, it records that as a discrepancy. The researchers applied this to real-world projects and found thousands of mismatches.
547.ww: Hidden bugs only reveal themselves when you compare two versions side by side with enough test cases. Most developers test one version or the other, not both; this gap lets discrepancies hide. Fuzzing (throwing random inputs at code to find breaks) combined with differential comparison (is this native output the same as WebAssembly?) surfaces issues that would otherwise silently corrupt data.
547.po: The survey found over 14,000 discrepancies across 64,000 test samples from a comprehensive benchmark, and 3,000+ in real-world projects. This quantifies the true scale of the porting problem and arms developers with concrete knowledge: if you port code to WebAssembly, you need differential testing, not just unit tests.

548.bp: Knowledge graphs—giant databases that map relationships between concepts (Einstein → scientist → physics) —contain a wealth of structured information. But using these graphs to answer complex multi-hop questions ('Who did Einstein work with that also contributed to quantum mechanics?') remains hard because the graph is enormous and the reasoning chain is long.
548.wh: A naive search would explore every possible path through a massive graph, which explodes in scale. More sophisticated methods focus on short paths but miss context: a connection might be technically shortest but semantically irrelevant. Also, when the language model encounters uncertainty, traditional systems just return the best-effort answer; they don't ask for clarification or refine the search dynamically.
548.ap: S-Path-RAG uses three layers: (1) a path-finding stage that explores multiple candidate paths through the graph, weighting them by semantic relevance rather than pure distance; (2) a learned ranker that scores which paths are most likely to answer the question; and (3) an iterative refinement loop where the language model can signal doubt ('I'm not confident about this step'), which triggers the system to modify its search or explore new parts of the graph. The system also compresses the paths into a compact format the language model can reason over efficiently.
548.ww: Semantic weighting focuses search on meaningful connections, not just short jumps. A learned ranker learns what paths humans actually need rather than guessing. Crucially, the iterative dialogue lets the language model actively participate in searching: instead of the system doing all the work upfront, they collaborate, with the model diagnosing what information is missing and the graph searcher filling gaps.
548.po: On multi-hop benchmarks, S-Path-RAG answers questions more accurately and uses fewer tokens (saving computation and cost). It also produces interpretable traces—you can see which graph paths led to each answer—making the system more trustworthy for high-stakes queries like medical or legal research.

549.bp: As large language models make more decisions—writing contracts, diagnosing illnesses, recommending policy—we need them to regulate their own behavior: to refuse harmful requests, to admit uncertainty, to push back on orders that contradict their values. Can an AI system govern itself, or does it need external control?
549.wh: Self-governance requires moral agency—the ability to understand right from wrong at a deep level, not just pattern-match training examples. It requires accountability: someone must answer for the system's decisions, and an AI can't truly answer to society. It requires grounding values in something beyond training data. These aren't engineering problems alone; they're philosophical.
549.ap: The paper analyzes three technical mechanisms that enable partial self-regulation: internal feedback loops (the model can check its own reasoning), embedded constraints (built-in refusals for certain harms), and meta-learning (learning to learn new values). It then argues that while these create operational self-regulation, they fall short of true governance because they lack authentic moral agency and genuine accountability.
549.ww: Self-monitoring works only if the model understands why a decision is harmful, not just that it was tagged 'bad' in training. An embedded refusal can block obvious harms but fails on novel scenarios. Without the ability to be held responsible by human society—which requires something more than computational process—self-governance remains performance, not genuine commitment.
549.po: The paper concludes that LLM self-governance should complement, not replace, human oversight. Technical safeguards help, but rely on humans to set values, interpret edge cases, and bear ultimate responsibility. This reframes the question from 'can machines self-govern?' to 'how do we partner with machines in governance systems that humans still anchor?'

550.bp: People send stickers (small expressive images) to convey emotion and intent in chat. But sticker collections are vast and diverse, and what's the right sticker for 'I'm thinking about what you said' or 'let's move on from this argument' is highly personal. When users search for stickers, the system fails if the stickers don't match their emotional intent.
550.wh: Sticker retrieval is a mismatch problem: the query is words ('I'm confused'), the sticker is an image, and what connects them is nebulous human meaning. New stickers and new query styles constantly appear, so the system must handle searches and images it's never seen. If the retriever memorizes specific stickers and specific phrases, it catastrophically fails on anything novel.
550.ap: XAlign-SR aligns the abstract communicative intent between text queries and visual stickers by learning a shared meaning space where both can be compared. Rather than treating text and image separately, it extracts the underlying intent (confusion, agreement, uncertainty) from both and measures how well they match. To address unseen cases, it learns this intent alignment in a way that generalizes to novel queries and stickers.
550.ww: Intent is invariant under variation—different ways of saying 'I'm confused' all share the same core meaning, and different stickers expressing confusion should cluster together. By learning to recognize this abstract meaning rather than memorizing surface forms, the system becomes robust to the constantly shifting landscape of how people express themselves and design stickers.
550.po: Tests on novel queries and stickers show XAlign-SR substantially outperforms baseline systems, correctly matching emotional intent even for queries and stickers the system never encountered during training. Users get better sticker recommendations, and the platform can ship new sticker packs without retraining.

551.bp: Aligning large language models with human values—making them helpful, honest, harmless—has become crucial. But people disagree on values: some prioritize free expression, others safety; some care about environmental impact, others cost. Can a single model be aligned with multiple, sometimes conflicting values?
551.wh: Training a separate model for each value trade-off (high freedom but low safety, vice versa, etc.) is prohibitively expensive. Merging models trained on different values often fails: the values don't blend smoothly; instead, they sabotage each other, and the merged model becomes mediocre at everything. A single training approach that respects all values simultaneously remains elusive.
551.ap: VC-Soup filters preference data to keep only examples where different values agree ('everyone thinks lying is bad'), then trains models on these consistent examples. These filtered models naturally blend better because they're built on common ground. Finally, it linearly combines the models, a technique that works well when the underlying models share similar internal structure (which the filtering ensures).
551.ww: Value conflicts are sharpest in contradictory examples: 'tell a comforting lie' versus 'always be truthful.' By removing examples where values clash and training on consensus examples, each model learns a 'pure' version of its value without being sabotaged by contradictions. The resulting models have more aligned internal structure, so simple averaging combines them cleanly.
551.po: The system achieves better trade-offs across values than prior methods. A single merged model now handles multiple conflicting priorities more gracefully than prior approaches required, without the expense of training separate models. This is a step toward systems that can serve diverse human communities, each with their own value priorities.

552.bp: Financial markets, communication networks, and social networks all change over time: connections appear and disappear, strengths shift. Predicting what edges (connections) will form next in these dynamic graphs—who will message whom, what stock will correlate with what—helps traders anticipate patterns, networks prepare capacity, and marketers find influencers.
552.wh: Graphs have structure at multiple scales: fast, minute-by-minute fluctuations (someone replies to a message); slower trends (friendships strengthen over weeks). Capturing all of these in a single model is hard. Also, the graph is huge (millions of nodes), so methods that require exploring every path explode in computation.
552.ap: TFWaveFormer uses a technique from signal processing (wavelet decomposition, which breaks signals into components at different speeds) combined with Transformer architecture (a modern way to learn relationships). The system decomposes the dynamic graph into multiple frequency bands (fast and slow changes) in parallel, processes each with adapted operations, and then fuses them. This replaces traditional time-series methods with learnable decomposition.
552.ww: Financial and social systems genuinely operate at multiple timescales: algorithm-driven trades happen in milliseconds; human relationships evolve over days. By decomposing the dynamics explicitly at each scale before reasoning, the model avoids trying to compress disparate phenomena into a single 'average' view. Each band gets specialized computation suited to its dynamics.
552.po: On benchmark datasets, TFWaveFormer predicts future edges more accurately and faster than competing Transformer and hybrid methods. The improvement is large enough to matter in real applications: better prediction helps traders react faster and networks allocate resources more efficiently.

553.bp: Social platforms like X (Twitter) contain billions of different users with vastly different ways of engaging. Some scroll silently, some reply to everything, some post constantly. These groups likely inhabit different information environments and respond differently to platform changes. Understanding who does what is foundational to fair platform design.
553.wh: Most research relies on surveys ('How often do you post?'), which are small-scale, biased toward engaged users, and missing the detailed behavioral ground truth. The platform has precise logs—how long someone viewed a post, when they liked, when they scrolled past—but hasn't been analyzed to map these behavioral nuances systematically.
553.ap: The researchers obtained detailed activity logs from 209 US X users over four weeks and identified patterns using latent profile analysis, a statistical technique that discovers natural groupings in behavior data. They found three groups: lurkers (60% of users, mostly scroll and view), interactors (32%, actively like and reply), and creators (7%, posting regularly).
553.ww: Behavior reveals deeper differences than demographics. The three groups don't just act differently; they encounter different content and politics. Lurkers and interactors skew young and Democratic; creators skew older and Republican, seeing more extreme content. This suggests that activity patterns and algorithmic exposure form a feedback loop: who you are as a user shapes what you see.
553.po: These findings argue that platform moderation and interventions can't be one-size-fits-all. Shadow-banning a creator affects them differently than it affects a lurker. Throttling recommendations hits different groups unequally. The paper provides a behavioral segmentation that platforms can use to design fairer, more targeted policies that account for these structural differences.

554.bp: Online moderation—deciding what content stays and what gets removed—has traditionally been gatekept by platforms themselves. But Bluesky allows users to publish their own moderation decisions (who they block), making the invisible visible. At scale, this reveals whether community-driven moderation actually works or devolves into mob rule.
554.wh: Blocking is a private action on most platforms, so we never see patterns: which accounts get blocked most? Do blocks reduce their influence? Can coordinated blocking silence minorities, or does it mostly target genuine harms? Without data, people argue about community moderation in the abstract; with data, we can measure its real effects.
554.ap: The researchers mapped 34 million accounts and their blocking relationships, including curated blocklists (like 'block all accounts matching pattern X'). They measured which accounts get blocked most, what behaviors correlate with blocking, and whether blocking actually reduces the visibility or activity of blocked accounts.
554.ww: Transparency reveals the mechanics of collective action. When millions of users independently block the same accounts, that's signal—it suggests genuine consensus on harm. Conversely, if blocks have minimal impact on visibility, we learn that blocking is performative, not effective. Data-driven analysis cuts through rhetoric.
554.po: The study found that community blocking is massive (orders of magnitude higher than official removals) and affects 90%+ of Bluesky content. However, blocks don't actually reduce the popularity of blocked accounts—they mostly create siloed views rather than true removal. Different blocklists target different types of accounts, suggesting pluralistic rather than monolithic moderation. This grounds debate about decentralized moderation in empirical reality: it works differently than centralized control, with both strengths and limitations.
